  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    const blurIn = (sel, t, d = 0.2) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(10px)" }, { opacity: 1, filter: "blur(0px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const blurOut = (sel, t, d = 0.2) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(8px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.in" }, t);
    const land = (sel, t, from = 1.3, d = 0.35) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: d, ease: "expo.out" }, t);
    const each = (sel, t, gap = 0.12, from = 1.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: 0.3, ease: "expo.out", stagger: gap }, t);
    const wipe = (sel, t, d = 0.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { clipPath: "inset(0 100% 0 0)" }, { clipPath: "inset(0 0% 0 0)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const dim = (sel, t, to = 0.3) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: to, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.inOut" }, t);
    blurIn("#s3-stage", 0, 0.25);

    land("#s3-r0", 3.07);
    blurIn("#s3-d0", 4.59);
    land("#s3-r1", 5.19);
    blurIn("#s3-d1", 5.39);
    land("#s3-r2", 5.67);
    blurIn("#s3-d2", 6.7);
    land("#s3-r3", 8.81);
    blurIn("#s3-d3", 9.79);

    blurOut("#s3-stage", 11.3, 0.25);
    window.__timelines["regions"] = tl;
  </script>
</template>

`videos/04-pointer-chains/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

`videos/04-pointer-chains/SCRIPT.md`:

```md
# Narration: Follow the Pointers

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–7.6) Your player moves to a new address on every run. Yet the game always finds it. How?
2. (7.6–15.7) It keeps a note in a fixed place: a pointer. A pointer is just a number, and that number is an address.
3. (15.7–24.2) Read the note, and you are standing at the start of the player. Health sits a fixed distance in: offset E C.
4. (24.2–31.0) So the recipe is: read the pointer, then add the offset. In that order.
5. (31.0–38.7) Add first and read second, and you land somewhere else entirely. That is the classic mistake.
6. (38.7–47.8) Real games chain several. Player points to weapon, weapon points to ammo. Read, add, repeat.
7. (47.8–55.0) If a link holds zero, stop. There is no player yet, and reading address zero crashes.
8. (55.0–62.9) A pointer chain is the path the game itself walks. Walk it the same way.

```

`videos/04-pointer-chains/build.py`:

```py
"""Video 4: Follow the Pointers (pointer chains).  Run: python build.py"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "tools"))
from kit import Scene, bar, build, card, cells, tile, txt  # noqa: E402,F401

INK = "#0B2A30"

scenes = [
    Scene("hook", "Your player moves to a new address on every run. Yet the game always finds it. How?",
          body=txt("@p-t", 190, 100, "a new address on every run", "h", fs=84)
          + tile("@p-p1", 250, 330, 340, 130, "player", 52) + txt("@p-a1", 250, 490, "0x0A3F2000", "m")
          + tile("@p-p2", 820, 470, 340, 130, "player", 52) + txt("@p-a2", 820, 630, "0x0B71C400", "m")
          + tile("@p-p3", 1340, 300, 340, 130, "player", 52) + txt("@p-a3", 1340, 460, "0x09E60800", "m")
          + txt("@p-q", 190, 820, '<span class="@p-acc">how does the game find it?</span>', "h", fs=90),
          js="""
    each(["#@p-p2", "#@p-a2"], <<new>>, 0.15);
    each(["#@p-p3", "#@p-a3"], <<every>>, 0.15);
    wipe("#@p-q", <<yet>>, 0.7);
"""),

    Scene("pointer", "It keeps a note in a fixed place: a pointer. A pointer is just a number, "
                     "and that number is an address.",
          body=txt("@p-l", 190, 210, "a fixed place", "m")
          + card("@p-s", 190, 300, 700, 130, "game.exe + 0x18AC00", 46, "soft")
          + card("@p-v", 190, 460, 700, 130, "0x0A3F2000", 60)
          + bar("@p-b", 890, 519, 210)
          + tile("@p-pl", 1100, 420, 560, 210, "player", 84)
          + txt("@p-at", 1100, 670, "at 0x0A3F2000", "m")
          + txt("@p-c", 0, 830, "a pointer is a number that is an address", "h", fs=70, w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-s", <<note>>);
    blurIn("#@p-l", <<fixed>>);
    land("#@p-v", <<number>>);
    wipe("#@p-b", <<address-0.5>>, 0.3);
    land("#@p-pl", <<address>>);
    blurIn("#@p-at", <<address+0.2>>);
    blurIn("#@p-c", <<pointer#2>>);
"""),

    Scene("struct", "Read the note, and you are standing at the start of the player. "
                    "Health sits a fixed distance in: offset E C.",
          body=txt("@p-h", 260, 150, "Player, starting at 0x0A3F2000", "m")
          + card("@p-f0", 260, 250, 700, 110, "+0x00 &nbsp; ...", 50)
          + card("@p-f1", 260, 380, 700, 110, "+0x04 &nbsp; ...", 50)
          + card("@p-f2", 260, 510, 700, 110, "+0xEC &nbsp; health = 100", 46, "on")
          + card("@p-f3", 260, 640, 700, 110, "+0xF0 &nbsp; armor", 50)
          + txt("@p-o", 1060, 440, '<span class="@p-acc">offset 0xEC</span>', "h", fs=110)
          + txt("@p-d", 1060, 590, "a fixed distance<br>from the start", "m"),
          js="""
    blurIn("#@p-h", <<start>>);
    each(["#@p-f0", "#@p-f1", "#@p-f3"], <<player>>, 0.12);
    land("#@p-f2", <<health>>);
    blurIn("#@p-d", <<fixed>>);
    land("#@p-o", <<offset>>);
"""),

    Scene("recipe", "So the recipe is: read the pointer, then add the offset. In that order.",
          body=txt("@p-f", 0, 300, '[game.exe + 0x18AC00] <span class="@p-acc">+ 0xEC</span>', "m", fs=100, color=INK, w=1920, align="center")
          + txt("@p-s1", 520, 520, "1. read the pointer", "m", fs=64)
          + txt("@p-s2", 520, 630, "2. add the offset", "m", fs=64)
          + txt("@p-c", 0, 820, '<span class="@p-acc">in that order</span>', "h", fs=90, w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-f", <<recipe>>, 1.15);
    blurIn("#@p-s1", <<read>>);
    blurIn("#@p-s2", <<add>>);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<order-0.4>>, 0.5);
"""),

    Scene("mistake", "Add first and read second, and you land somewhere else entirely. That is the classic mistake.",
          body=txt("@p-gl", 288, 180, "read, then add", "m")
          + txt("@p-g", 288, 260, '[game.exe + 0x18AC00] <span class="@p-acc">+ 0xEC</span>', "m", fs=80, color=INK)
          + txt("@p-bl", 288, 520, "add, then read: somewhere else", "m")
          + txt("@p-b", 288, 600, "[game.exe + 0x18AC00 + 0xEC]", "m", fs=80, color="#6A9188")
          + bar("@p-x", 270, 642, 1390, 14)
          + txt("@p-c", 0, 830, "the classic mistake", "h", fs=90, w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    blurIn("#@p-b", <<add>>);
    blurIn("#@p-bl", <<somewhere>>);
    wipe("#@p-x", <<classic-0.3>>, 0.35);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<classic>>, 0.5);
"""),

    Scene("chain", "Real games chain several. Player points to weapon, weapon points to ammo. Read, add, repeat.",
          body=card("@p-c1", 190, 380, 400, 160, "Player", 60)
          + txt("@p-o1", 600, 300, "+0x364", "m", fs=46) + bar("@p-b1", 590, 454, 170)
          + card("@p-c2", 760, 380, 400, 160, "Weapon", 60)
          + txt("@p-o2", 1178, 300, "+0x14", "m", fs=46) + bar("@p-b2", 1160, 454, 170)
          + card("@p-c3", 1330, 380, 400, 160, "Ammo: 20", 56, "on")
          + txt("@p-f", 0, 650, "[[game.exe + 0x18AC00] + 0x364] + 0x14", "m", fs=60, color=INK, w=1920, align="center")
          + txt("@p-r", 0, 820, "read, add, repeat", "h", fs=90, w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-c1", <<player>>);
    wipe("#@p-b1", <<points>>, 0.25);
    blurIn("#@p-o1", <<points>>);
    land("#@p-c2", <<weapon>>);
    wipe("#@p-b2", <<points#2>>, 0.25);
    blurIn("#@p-o2", <<points#2>>);
    land("#@p-c3", <<ammo>>);
    blurIn("#@p-f", <<read-0.6>>);
    wipe("#@p-r", <<read>>, 0.8);
"""),

    Scene("null", "If a link holds zero, stop. There is no player yet, and reading address zero crashes.",
          body=card("@p-s", 190, 250, 700, 130, "game.exe + 0x18AC00", 46, "soft")
          + card("@p-v", 190, 410, 700, 130, "0x00000000", 60, "on")
          + bar("@p-b", 890, 469, 210)
          + card("@p-n", 1100, 380, 560, 190, "no player yet", 52, "soft")
          + txt("@p-st", 190, 640, '<span class="@p-acc">stop.</span>', "h", fs=150)
          + txt("@p-m", 190, 850, "reading address 0 crashes the program", "m"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-v", <<zero>>);
    land("#@p-st", <<stop>>);
    wipe("#@p-b", <<no-0.3>>, 0.25);
    blurIn("#@p-n", <<no>>);
    blurIn("#@p-m", <<reading>>);
"""),

    Scene("claim", "A pointer chain is the path the game itself walks. Walk it the same way.",
          body=card("@p-c1", 192, 200, 300, 110, "base", 46, "soft") + bar("@p-b1", 492, 249, 80)
          + card("@p-c2", 572, 200, 300, 110, "+ offset", 46) + bar("@p-b2", 872, 249, 80)
          + card("@p-c3", 952, 200, 300, 110, "value", 46, "on")
          + txt("@p-a", 192, 400, "A pointer chain is the<br>path the game walks.", "h", fs=110)
          + txt("@p-c", 192, 680, '<span class="@p-acc">Walk it the same way.</span>', "h", fs=110),
          js="""
    each(["#@p-c1", "#@p-b1", "#@p-c2", "#@p-b2", "#@p-c3"], 0.3, 0.1, 1.1);
    wipe("#@p-a", <<pointer>>, 0.9);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<walk-0.2>>, 0.6);
"""),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    build(__file__, scenes, "Follow the Pointers")

```

    .s6-card.soft { background: #CFE9DF; }
    .s6-bar { position: absolute; background: #0B2A30; }
  </style>
  <div id="root" data-composition-id="chain" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
    <div id="s6-stage" class="clip s6-stage" data-start="0" data-duration="9.1">
      <div id="s6-c1" class="s6-card " style="left: 190px; top: 380px; width: 400px; height: 160px; line-height: 144px; font-size: 60px">Player</div>
      <div id="s6-o1" class="s6-m" style="left: 600px; top: 300px; font-size: 46px">+0x364</div>
      <div id="s6-b1" class="s6-bar" style="left: 590px; top: 454px; width: 170px; height: 12px"></div>
      <div id="s6-c2" class="s6-card " style="left: 760px; top: 380px; width: 400px; height: 160px; line-height: 144px; font-size: 60px">Weapon</div>
      <div id="s6-o2" class="s6-m" style="left: 1178px; top: 300px; font-size: 46px">+0x14</div>
      <div id="s6-b2" class="s6-bar" style="left: 1160px; top: 454px; width: 170px; height: 12px"></div>

      <div id="s6-r" class="s6-h" style="left: 0px; top: 820px; font-size: 90px; width: 1920px; text-align: center">read, add, repeat</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    const blurIn = (sel, t, d = 0.2) =>

      <div id="s2-v" class="s2-card " style="left: 190px; top: 460px; width: 700px; height: 130px; line-height: 114px; font-size: 60px">0x0A3F2000</div>
      <div id="s2-b" class="s2-bar" style="left: 890px; top: 519px; width: 210px; height: 12px"></div>
      <div id="s2-pl" class="s2-tile" style="left: 1100px; top: 420px; width: 560px; height: 210px; line-height: 186px; font-size: 84px">player</div>
      <div id="s2-at" class="s2-m" style="left: 1100px; top: 670px">at 0x0A3F2000</div>
      <div id="s2-c" class="s2-h" style="left: 0px; top: 830px; font-size: 70px; width: 1920px; text-align: center">a pointer is a number that is an address</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    const blurIn = (sel, t, d = 0.2) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(10px)" }, { opacity: 1, filter: "blur(0px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const blurOut = (sel, t, d = 0.2) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(8px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.in" }, t);
    const land = (sel, t, from = 1.3, d = 0.35) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: d, ease: "expo.out" }, t);
    const each = (sel, t, gap = 0.12, from = 1.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: 0.3, ease: "expo.out", stagger: gap }, t);
    const wipe = (sel, t, d = 0.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { clipPath: "inset(0 100% 0 0)" }, { clipPath: "inset(0 0% 0 0)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const dim = (sel, t, to = 0.3) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: to, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.inOut" }, t);
    blurIn("#s2-stage", 0, 0.25);

    land("#s2-s", 0.93);
    blurIn("#s2-l", 1.47);
    land("#s2-v", 4.54);
    wipe("#s2-b", 5.89, 0.3);
    land("#s2-pl", 6.39);
    blurIn("#s2-at", 6.59);
    blurIn("#s2-c", 3.59);

    blurOut("#s2-stage", 7.8, 0.25);
    window.__timelines["pointer"] = tl;

`videos/05-reading-assembly/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

`videos/05-reading-assembly/SCRIPT.md`:

```md
# Narration: Read One Line of Assembly

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–8.2) Somewhere in the game, one instruction takes away your health. Read that one line, and you understand the whole trick.
2. (8.2–17.0) Here it is. Move, into the memory at E B X plus E C, the value of E A X.
3. (17.0–25.0) Destination comes first, source second. So this line copies E A X into something.
4. (25.0–32.2) Square brackets mean memory. Not the register itself, but the address stored inside it.
5. (32.2–40.2) E B X holds the start of the player. E C is the offset of health. One line just told you both.
6. (40.2–47.9) Two lines earlier, a subtract: health minus damage. Then this line stores the result.
7. (47.9–57.6) Replace the store with no-ops, the instruction that does nothing, and health stops dropping. Six bytes out, six no-ops in.
8. (57.6–65.6) But careful. The same code runs for enemies too. E B X is whoever just got hit.
9. (65.6–74.4) Destination, brackets, offset. Read those three, and you can read the line.

```

`videos/05-reading-assembly/build.py`:

```py
"""Video 5: Read One Line of Assembly.  Run: python build.py"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "tools"))
from kit import Scene, arena, bar, build, card, cells, tile, txt  # noqa: E402,F401

INK = "#0B2A30"
SPAN = "\n    .@p-m span { display: inline-block; }\n"


def line(y, fs=120):
    """The instruction, 19 characters wide, starting at x=276 when fs=120."""
    return txt("@p-ln", 276, y, '<span id="@p-x1">mov</span> <span id="@p-x2">[ebx+0xEC]</span>, <span id="@p-x3">eax</span>',
               "m", fs=fs, color=INK)


scenes = [
    Scene("hook", "Somewhere in the game, one instruction takes away your health. "
                  "Read that one line, and you understand the whole trick.",
          bg="arena",
          body=arena("100")
          + txt("@p-d", 640, 640, '-25', "h", fs=170)
          + card("@p-q", 1010, 150, 720, 120, "one instruction", 56)
          + card("@p-r", 1010, 310, 720, 120, "? ? ? &nbsp; ? ? ?", 60, "on"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-q", <<instruction-0.3>>);
    land("#@p-d", <<takes>>, 1.6);
    tl.fromTo("#@p-hudn", { scale: 1 }, { scale: 0.92, duration: 0.15, ease: "power2.out", yoyo: true, repeat: 1 }, <<takes>>);
    land("#@p-r", <<read>>);
    tl.fromTo("#@p-r", { rotation: 0 }, { rotation: -3, duration: 0.25, ease: "power2.out" }, <<whole>>);
"""),

    Scene("theline", "Here it is. Move, into the memory at E B X plus E C, the value of E A X.",
          css=SPAN,
          body=line(400) + txt("@p-c", 276, 600, "one line of assembly", "m"),
          js="""
    blurIn("#@p-c", <<here>>);
    blurIn("#@p-x1", <<move>>);
    blurIn("#@p-x2", <<memory>>);
    blurIn("#@p-x3", <<value>>);
"""),

    Scene("order", "Destination comes first, source second. So this line copies E A X into something.",
          css=SPAN,
          body=line(340)
          + bar("@p-b1", 564, 500, 720) + txt("@p-l1", 564, 530, "destination", "m")
          + bar("@p-b2", 1428, 500, 216) + txt("@p-l2", 1428, 530, "source", "m")
          + txt("@p-c", 0, 800, "destination first, source second", "h", fs=80, w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    wipe("#@p-b1", <<destination>>, 0.3);
    blurIn("#@p-l1", <<destination>>);
    wipe("#@p-b2", <<source>>, 0.3);
    blurIn("#@p-l2", <<source>>);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<copies-0.3>>, 0.7);
"""),

    Scene("brackets", "Square brackets mean memory. Not the register itself, but the address stored inside it.",
          css=SPAN + "\n    .@p-card { line-height: 1.25 !important; }\n",
          body=line(170)
          + txt("@p-c", 276, 370, '<span class="@p-acc">[ ]</span> means memory', "h", fs=90)
          + txt("@p-reg", 276, 620, "ebx = 0x0A3F2000", "m", fs=60, color=INK)
          + bar("@p-b", 880, 652, 200)

      <div id="s6-c2" class="s6-card " style="left: 190px; top: 400px; width: 900px; height: 130px; line-height: 114px; font-size: 58px">sub eax, edi</div>
      <div id="s6-n2" class="s6-m" style="left: 1150px; top: 432px">subtract the damage</div>
      <div id="s6-c3" class="s6-card on" style="left: 190px; top: 570px; width: 900px; height: 130px; line-height: 114px; font-size: 58px">mov [ebx+0xEC], eax</div>
      <div id="s6-n3" class="s6-m" style="left: 1150px; top: 602px">store the result</div>
      <div id="s6-c" class="s6-h" style="left: 190px; top: 810px; font-size: 84px">read, subtract, store</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    const blurIn = (sel, t, d = 0.2) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(10px)" }, { opacity: 1, filter: "blur(0px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const blurOut = (sel, t, d = 0.2) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(8px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.in" }, t);
    const land = (sel, t, from = 1.3, d = 0.35) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: d, ease: "expo.out" }, t);
    const each = (sel, t, gap = 0.12, from = 1.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: 0.3, ease: "expo.out", stagger: gap }, t);
    const wipe = (sel, t, d = 0.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { clipPath: "inset(0 100% 0 0)" }, { clipPath: "inset(0 0% 0 0)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const dim = (sel, t, to = 0.3) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: to, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.inOut" }, t);
    blurIn("#s6-stage", 0, 0.25);

    land("#s6-c1", 0.5);
    blurIn("#s6-n1", 1.09);
    land("#s6-c2", 1.65);
    blurIn("#s6-n2", 3.03);
    blurIn("#s6-n3", 5.7);
    wipe("#s6-c", 5.78, 0.6);

    blurOut("#s6-stage", 7.4, 0.25);
    window.__timelines["three"] = tl;
  </script>
</template>

`videos/06-hex-editing/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

`videos/06-hex-editing/SCRIPT.md`:

```md
# Narration: Edit a Save File, Byte by Byte

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–10.5) A save file is just bytes on disk. No debugger, no running game. Open it in a hex editor, and your gold is sitting right there.
2. (10.5–19.2) Three columns. The offset: how far from the start. The bytes. And the same bytes as text.
3. (19.2–30.6) Read it like memory. The letters S A V E. Then one hundred, as a whole number. Then E eight, zero three: one thousand gold.
4. (30.6–40.7) To find a value, save with one thousand gold, then with twelve fifty, and compare the two files. The bytes that changed are yours.
5. (40.7–48.9) Overwrite those four bytes with the biggest number they can hold. Save the file, load the game, and you are rich.
6. (48.9–61.4) Two traps. Never insert bytes, only overwrite, or everything after them shifts. And some games store a checksum, so an edited save looks corrupt.
7. (61.4–70.5) So back up the file first. And remember: a file is just memory that sits still.

```

`videos/06-hex-editing/build.py`:

```py
"""Video 6: Edit a Save File, Byte by Byte (hex editing).  Run: python build.py"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "tools"))
from kit import Scene, bar, build, card, cells, tile, txt  # noqa: E402,F401

INK = "#0B2A30"
SPAN = "\n    .@p-m span { display: inline-block; }\n    .@p-of { color: #6A9188; }\n"


def rows(y):
    """Three hex-editor rows, 8 bytes each. Columns at fs=56: offset x=180, bytes x=516, text x=1356."""
    data = [
        ("00000000", '<span id="@p-g1">53 41 56 45</span> 01 00 00 00', "SAVE...."),
        ("00000008", '<span id="@p-g2">64 00 00 00</span> <span id="@p-g3">E8 03 00 00</span>', "d...&egrave;..."),
        ("00000010", "42 6F 62 00 00 00 00 00", "Bob....."),
    ]
    out = ""
    for i, (off, by, tx) in enumerate(data):
        out += txt(f"@p-r{i}", 180, y + i * 96,
                   f'<span class="@p-of">{off}</span>&nbsp;&nbsp;{by}&nbsp;&nbsp;<span class="@p-of">{tx}</span>',
                   "m", fs=56, color=INK)
    return out


HI = '{ backgroundColor: "#FF5A1F", color: "#ffffff", duration: 0.25, ease: "power2.out" }'

scenes = [
    Scene("hook", "A save file is just bytes on disk. No debugger, no running game. "
                  "Open it in a hex editor, and your gold is sitting right there.",
          css=SPAN,
          body=txt("@p-t", 180, 150, "save.dat", "h", fs=96) + rows(330)
          + txt("@p-c", 180, 720, '<span class="@p-acc">your gold: 1000</span>', "h", fs=110),
          js=f"""
    wipe("#@p-r0", <<bytes>>, 0.4);
    wipe("#@p-r1", <<debugger>>, 0.4);
    wipe("#@p-r2", <<running>>, 0.4);
    tl.fromTo("#@p-t", {{ scale: 1 }}, {{ scale: 1.06, duration: 0.2, ease: "power2.out", yoyo: true, repeat: 1 }}, <<open>>);
    tl.to("#@p-g3", {HI}, <<gold>>);
    land("#@p-c", <<gold+0.2>>);
"""),

    Scene("columns", "Three columns. The offset: how far from the start. The bytes. And the same bytes as text.",
          css=SPAN,
          body=rows(250)
          + bar("@p-b1", 180, 560, 269) + txt("@p-l1", 180, 590, "offset", "m")
          + bar("@p-b2", 516, 560, 773) + txt("@p-l2", 516, 590, "the bytes, in hex", "m")
          + bar("@p-b3", 1356, 560, 269) + txt("@p-l3", 1356, 590, "as text", "m")
          + txt("@p-c", 180, 780, "how far from the start of the file", "m"),
          js="""
    wipe("#@p-b1", <<offset>>, 0.3);
    blurIn("#@p-l1", <<offset>>);
    blurIn("#@p-c", <<far>>);
    wipe("#@p-b2", <<bytes>>, 0.4);
    blurIn("#@p-l2", <<bytes>>);
    wipe("#@p-b3", <<text>>, 0.3);
    blurIn("#@p-l3", <<text>>);
"""),

    Scene("read", "Read it like memory. The letters S A V E. Then one hundred, as a whole number. "
                  "Then E eight, zero three: one thousand gold.",
          css=SPAN,
          body=rows(200)
          + card("@p-c1", 180, 600, 420, 140, "SAVE", 64) + txt("@p-m1", 180, 770, "a text marker", "m", fs=44)
          + card("@p-c2", 690, 600, 420, 140, "100", 64) + txt("@p-m2", 690, 770, "health, 4 bytes", "m", fs=44)
          + card("@p-c3", 1200, 600, 420, 140, "1000", 64, "on") + txt("@p-m3", 1200, 770, "gold, small end first", "m", fs=44),
          js=f"""
    tl.to("#@p-g1", {{ backgroundColor: "#0B2A30", color: "#ffffff", duration: 0.25 }}, <<letters>>);
    each(["#@p-c1", "#@p-m1"], <<letters+0.3>>, 0.15);
    tl.to("#@p-g2", {{ backgroundColor: "#0B2A30", color: "#ffffff", duration: 0.25 }}, <<hundred-0.4>>);
    each(["#@p-c2", "#@p-m2"], <<hundred>>, 0.15);
    tl.to("#@p-g3", {HI}, <<eight>>);
    each(["#@p-c3", "#@p-m3"], <<thousand>>, 0.15);
"""),

    Scene("compare", "To find a value, save with one thousand gold, then with twelve fifty, and compare the two files. "
                     "The bytes that changed are yours.",
          body=txt("@p-l1", 190, 300, "save 1<br>1000 gold", "m")
          + cells("@p-a", 720, 270, ["E8", "03", "00", "00"], 190, 26, on={0, 1})
          + txt("@p-l2", 190, 560, "save 2<br>1250 gold", "m")
          + cells("@p-b", 720, 530, ["E2", "04", "00", "00"], 190, 26, on={0, 1})
          + txt("@p-c", 0, 820, "what changed is yours", "h", fs=90, w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    blurIn("#@p-l1", <<thousand-0.5>>);
    each(".c-@p-a", <<thousand>>, 0.1);
    blurIn("#@p-l2", <<then>>);
    each(".c-@p-b", <<twelve>>, 0.1);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<changed-0.3>>, 0.6);
"""),

    Scene("edit", "Overwrite those four bytes with the biggest number they can hold. Save the file, load the game, "
                  "and you are rich.",
          body=txt("@p-l1", 190, 215, "before", "m")
          + cells("@p-a", 720, 170, ["E8", "03", "00", "00"], 170, 24)
          + txt("@p-l2", 190, 445, "after", "m")
          + cells("@p-b", 720, 400, ["FF", "FF", "FF", "7F"], 170, 24, on={0, 1, 2, 3})
          + txt("@p-n", 0, 650, '<span class="@p-acc">2,147,483,647</span>', "h", fs=180, w=1920, align="center")
          + txt("@p-c", 0, 870, "gold", "m", w=1920, align="center"),
          js="""
    blurIn("#@p-l2", <<overwrite>>);
    each(".c-@p-b", <<overwrite+0.3>>, 0.3);
    dim(".c-@p-a", <<biggest>>, 0.35);
    land("#@p-n", <<load>>, 1.2);
    blurIn("#@p-c", <<rich>>);
"""),

    Scene("traps", "Two traps. Never insert bytes, only overwrite, or everything after them shifts. "
                   "And some games store a checksum, so an edited save looks corrupt.",
          body=txt("@p-t", 190, 100, "two traps", "h", fs=96)
          + card("@p-a", 190, 300, 720, 150, "overwrite, never insert", 46, "on")
          + txt("@p-am", 190, 480, "one extra byte shifts<br>everything after it", "m")
          + card("@p-b", 1010, 300, 720, 150, "checksum", 60, "on")
          + txt("@p-bm", 1010, 480, "the game notices the edit:<br>&quot;save corrupted&quot;", "m"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-a", <<insert-0.5>>);
    blurIn("#@p-am", <<shifts-0.6>>);
    land("#@p-b", <<checksum-0.3>>);
    blurIn("#@p-bm", <<corrupt-0.8>>);
"""),

    Scene("claim", "So back up the file first. And remember: a file is just memory that sits still.",
          body=cells("@p-b", 192, 190, ["E8", "03", "00", "00"], 120, 18, on={0, 1})
          + txt("@p-a", 192, 400, "Back up first.", "h", fs=118)
          + txt("@p-c", 192, 540, '<span class="@p-acc">A file is memory that sits still.</span>', "h", fs=92),
          js="""
    each(".c-@p-b", 0.3, 0.08);
    wipe("#@p-a", <<back>>, 0.5);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<file#2-0.2>>, 0.7);
"""),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    build(__file__, scenes, "Edit a Save File, Byte by Byte")

```

`videos/06-hex-editing/compositions/claim.html`:

```html
<template>
  <style>
    #root { position: absolute; inset: 0; overflow: hidden; background-color: #E4F2EC;
      background-image:
        linear-gradient(#9CCFC0 3px, transparent 3px), linear-gradient(90deg, #9CCFC0 3px, transparent 3px),

`videos/07-calling-conventions/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

`videos/07-calling-conventions/CLAUDE.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

`videos/07-calling-conventions/SCRIPT.md`:

```md
# Narration: Where Do the Arguments Go?

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–8.9) You found a function in the game. To understand it, or to call it yourself, you need to know one thing: where do its arguments go?
2. (8.9–16.8) In thirty-two bit code, they go on the stack. Pushed right to left, so the first argument ends up on top.
3. (16.8–28.5) Inside the function, E B P plus eight is the first argument. Plus twelve is the second. And E B P minus four is a local variable.
4. (28.5–43.6) Who cleans the stack afterwards? In the C convention, the caller does: you see an add to E S P right after the call. In the Windows convention, the function does: it ends with a return that pops its own arguments.
5. (43.6–54.7) C plus plus methods add one more thing: the object itself travels in E C X. Find what loads E C X before a call, and you have found the player.
6. (54.7–69.6) Sixty-four bit Windows has one rule for everyone. The first four arguments ride in registers: R C X, R D X, R eight and R nine. The result comes back in R A X.
7. (69.6–78.5) Stack or registers. Once you know where the arguments go, you can read any call.

```
