`videos/08-inside-an-exe/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

`videos/08-inside-an-exe/SCRIPT.md`:

```md
# Narration: What's Inside an EXE

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–10.8) Double-click a game, and Windows has to answer two questions. Where does this file go in memory? And what does it need? Both answers are inside the file.
2. (10.8–22.6) Every Windows program starts with two letters, M Z. A little further in come the headers: a table of contents for the whole file. After them, the sections.
3. (22.6–33.4) The sections are the body of the file. Dot text holds the code. Dot data holds the variables. Each one gets its own permissions when it is loaded.
4. (33.4–43.7) The headers name a preferred address: the image base. Add an offset from it, called an R V A, and you have a real address in memory.
5. (43.7–54.5) A game does not contain Windows. It only lists the functions it needs, in the import table. Windows fills in the real addresses at load time.
6. (54.5–66.6) So read the imports, and the file tells on itself. Open process, read process memory, write process memory: this program reaches into other programs.
7. (66.6–75.1) An executable is a map of itself. Learn to read the map before you read the code.

```

`videos/08-inside-an-exe/build.py`:

```py
"""Video 8: What's Inside an EXE (PE files, imports).  Run: python build.py"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "tools"))
from kit import Scene, bar, build, card, cells, tile, txt  # noqa: E402,F401

INK = "#0B2A30"

scenes = [
    Scene("hook", "Double-click a game, and Windows has to answer two questions. Where does this file go in memory? "
                  "And what does it need? Both answers are inside the file.",
          body=tile("@p-g", 190, 300, 620, 300, "game.exe", 90)
          + card("@p-q1", 960, 290, 760, 140, "where does it load?", 50)
          + card("@p-q2", 960, 470, 760, 140, "what does it need?", 50)
          + txt("@p-c", 190, 760, "both answers are inside the file", "h", fs=84),
          js="""
    tl.fromTo("#@p-g", { scale: 1 }, { scale: 0.94, duration: 0.1, ease: "power2.out", yoyo: true, repeat: 3 }, 0.5);
    land("#@p-q1", <<where>>);
    land("#@p-q2", <<what>>);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<both>>, 0.7);
"""),

    Scene("headers", "Every Windows program starts with two letters, M Z. A little further in come the headers: "
                     "a table of contents for the whole file. After them, the sections.",
          body=card("@p-r0", 260, 130, 620, 110, "MZ", 60, "on") + txt("@p-d0", 960, 155, "the first two bytes", "m")
          + card("@p-r1", 260, 270, 620, 150, "PE headers", 56) + txt("@p-d1", 960, 315, "the table of contents", "m")
          + card("@p-r2", 260, 450, 620, 110, "section table", 52) + txt("@p-d2", 960, 475, "one row per section", "m")
          + card("@p-r3", 260, 590, 620, 100, ".text", 50, "soft") + card("@p-r4", 260, 710, 620, 100, ".rdata", 50, "soft")
          + card("@p-r5", 260, 830, 620, 100, ".data", 50, "soft") + txt("@p-d3", 960, 730, "the sections", "m"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-r0", <<letters>>);
    blurIn("#@p-d0", <<letters+0.4>>);
    land("#@p-r1", <<headers>>);
    blurIn("#@p-d1", <<table>>);
    land("#@p-r2", <<contents>>);
    blurIn("#@p-d2", <<contents+0.3>>);
    each(["#@p-r3", "#@p-r4", "#@p-r5"], <<sections-0.3>>, 0.15);
    blurIn("#@p-d3", <<sections>>);
"""),

    Scene("sections", "The sections are the body of the file. Dot text holds the code. Dot data holds the variables. "
                      "Each one gets its own permissions when it is loaded.",
          body=txt("@p-t", 190, 90, "the sections", "h", fs=90)
          + card("@p-n0", 190, 280, 360, 130, ".text", 60) + txt("@p-m0", 610, 315, "the code", "m")
          + card("@p-p0", 1330, 280, 300, 130, "R X", 64, "on")
          + card("@p-n1", 190, 480, 360, 130, ".data", 60) + txt("@p-m1", 610, 515, "the variables", "m")
          + card("@p-p1", 1330, 480, 300, 130, "R W", 64, "on")
          + card("@p-n2", 190, 680, 360, 130, ".rdata", 60) + txt("@p-m2", 610, 715, "constants and imports", "m")
          + card("@p-p2", 1330, 680, 300, 130, "R", 64, "on"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-n0", <<text>>);
    blurIn("#@p-m0", <<code>>);
    land("#@p-n1", <<data>>);
    blurIn("#@p-m1", <<variables>>);
    each(["#@p-n2", "#@p-m2"], <<variables+0.6>>, 0.15);
    each(["#@p-p0", "#@p-p1", "#@p-p2"], <<permissions-0.3>>, 0.2);
"""),

    Scene("base", "The headers name a preferred address: the image base. Add an offset from it, called an R V A, "
                  "and you have a real address in memory.",
          body=card("@p-a", 190, 260, 620, 150, "0x00400000", 64) + txt("@p-am", 190, 440, "ImageBase", "m")
          + txt("@p-plus", 850, 280, "+", "h", fs=110)
          + card("@p-b", 960, 260, 420, 150, "0x1530", 64, "on") + txt("@p-bm", 960, 440, "RVA: offset from the base", "m")
          + tile("@p-r", 190, 640, 800, 190, "0x00401530", 90) + txt("@p-rm", 1050, 700, "a real address<br>in memory", "m"),
          js="""
    land("#@p-a", <<preferred>>);
    blurIn("#@p-am", <<base>>);
    blurIn("#@p-plus", <<add>>);
    land("#@p-b", <<offset>>);
    blurIn("#@p-bm", <<called>>);
    land("#@p-r", <<real-0.4>>);
    blurIn("#@p-rm", <<real>>);
"""),

    Scene("imports", "A game does not contain Windows. It only lists the functions it needs, in the import table. "
                     "Windows fills in the real addresses at load time.",
          body=txt("@p-t", 190, 90, "the import table", "h", fs=90)
          + card("@p-n0", 190, 290, 760, 120, "ReadFile", 52) + card("@p-n1", 190, 440, 760, 120, "CreateWindowExA", 52)
          + card("@p-n2", 190, 590, 760, 120, "Direct3DCreate9", 52)
          + bar("@p-b0", 950, 344, 110) + bar("@p-b1", 950, 494, 110) + bar("@p-b2", 950, 644, 110)
          + card("@p-a0", 1060, 290, 620, 120, "0x76A31C20", 52, "on") + card("@p-a1", 1060, 440, 620, 120, "0x75E2B410", 52, "on")
          + card("@p-a2", 1060, 590, 620, 120, "0x6F4C1A90", 52, "on")
          + txt("@p-c", 190, 790, "names in the file, addresses at load time (examples)", "m", fs=40),
          js="""
    wipe("#@p-t", <<import-0.3>>, 0.6);
    each(["#@p-n0", "#@p-n1", "#@p-n2"], <<lists>>, 0.3);
    each(["#@p-b0", "#@p-b1", "#@p-b2"], <<fills>>, 0.15, 1);
    each(["#@p-a0", "#@p-a1", "#@p-a2"], <<fills+0.2>>, 0.25);
    blurIn("#@p-c", <<lists+0.9>>);
"""),

    Scene("tell", "So read the imports, and the file tells on itself. Open process, read process memory, "
                  "write process memory: this program reaches into other programs.",
          body=txt("@p-t", 190, 90, "the imports tell on the file", "h", fs=84)
          + card("@p-n0", 190, 280, 900, 120, "OpenProcess", 54) + card("@p-n1", 190, 430, 900, 120, "ReadProcessMemory", 54)
          + card("@p-n2", 190, 580, 900, 120, "WriteProcessMemory", 54)
          + tile("@p-k", 190, 770, 1300, 160, "reaches into other programs", 60),
          js="""
    wipe("#@p-t", <<tells-0.5>>, 0.6);
    land("#@p-n0", <<open>>);
    land("#@p-n1", <<read#2>>);
    land("#@p-n2", <<write>>);
    land("#@p-k", <<reaches-0.3>>, 1.1);
"""),

    Scene("claim", "An executable is a map of itself. Learn to read the map before you read the code.",
          body=card("@p-a1", 192, 200, 260, 110, "headers", 44, "soft") + card("@p-a2", 480, 200, 260, 110, "sections", 44)
          + card("@p-a3", 768, 200, 260, 110, "imports", 44, "on")
          + txt("@p-a", 192, 400, "An EXE is a map of itself.", "h", fs=110)
          + txt("@p-c", 192, 540, '<span class="@p-acc">Read the map before the code.</span>', "h", fs=96),
          js="""
    each(["#@p-a1", "#@p-a2", "#@p-a3"], 0.3, 0.12);
    wipe("#@p-a", <<executable-0.3>>, 0.8);
    wipe("#@p-c", <<learn>>, 0.8);
"""),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    build(__file__, scenes, "What's Inside an EXE")

  </style>
  <div id="root" data-composition-id="base" data-width="1920" data-height="1080">
    <div id="s4-stage" class="clip s4-stage" data-start="0" data-duration="10.3">
      <div id="s4-a" class="s4-card " style="left: 190px; top: 260px; width: 620px; height: 150px; line-height: 134px; font-size: 64px">0x00400000</div>
      <div id="s4-am" class="s4-m" style="left: 190px; top: 440px">ImageBase</div>
      <div id="s4-plus" class="s4-h" style="left: 850px; top: 280px; font-size: 110px">+</div>

  <script>
    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    const blurIn = (sel, t, d = 0.2) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(10px)" }, { opacity: 1, filter: "blur(0px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const blurOut = (sel, t, d = 0.2) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(8px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.in" }, t);
    const land = (sel, t, from = 1.3, d = 0.35) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: d, ease: "expo.out" }, t);
    const each = (sel, t, gap = 0.12, from = 1.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: 0.3, ease: "expo.out", stagger: gap }, t);
    const wipe = (sel, t, d = 0.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { clipPath: "inset(0 100% 0 0)" }, { clipPath: "inset(0 0% 0 0)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const dim = (sel, t, to = 0.3) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: to, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.inOut" }, t);
    blurIn("#s4-stage", 0, 0.25);

    land("#s4-a", 1.52);
    blurIn("#s4-am", 3.46);
    blurIn("#s4-plus", 4.37);
    land("#s4-b", 4.67);
    blurIn("#s4-bm", 5.74);
    land("#s4-r", 7.49);
    blurIn("#s4-rm", 7.89);

    blurOut("#s4-stage", 10.0, 0.25);
    window.__timelines["base"] = tl;
  </script>
</template>

    const tl = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
    const blurIn = (sel, t, d = 0.2) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(10px)" }, { opacity: 1, filter: "blur(0px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const blurOut = (sel, t, d = 0.2) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: 0, filter: "blur(8px)", duration: d, ease: "power2.in" }, t);
    const land = (sel, t, from = 1.3, d = 0.35) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: d, ease: "expo.out" }, t);
    const each = (sel, t, gap = 0.12, from = 1.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { opacity: 0, scale: from }, { opacity: 1, scale: 1, duration: 0.3, ease: "expo.out", stagger: gap }, t);
    const wipe = (sel, t, d = 0.3) =>
      tl.fromTo(sel, { clipPath: "inset(0 100% 0 0)" }, { clipPath: "inset(0 0% 0 0)", duration: d, ease: "power2.out" }, t);
    const dim = (sel, t, to = 0.3) => tl.to(sel, { opacity: to, duration: 0.3, ease: "power2.inOut" }, t);
    blurIn("#s6-stage", 0, 0.25);

    wipe("#s6-t", 2.18, 0.6);
    land("#s6-n0", 4.11);
    land("#s6-n1", 5.43);
    land("#s6-n2", 6.86);
    land("#s6-k", 9.01, 1.1);

    blurOut("#s6-stage", 11.8, 0.25);
    window.__timelines["tell"] = tl;
  </script>

`videos/EPISODES.md`:

```md
# Game Hacking from Scratch: how an episode is made

The long YouTube series of this repo. One folder per episode: `videos/epNN-<slug>/`. Episodes 1 and 2 are the reference:
read `ep01-bytes-behind-the-health-bar/build.py` and `ep02-why-the-address-changes/build.py` before writing a new one.

## The format the owner chose

- **One continuous video, 7 to 9 minutes.** No lesson title cards, no chapter cards, no mini-game, no recap of "lesson 1.2".
  One short title scene after the cold open, then straight teaching, scene after scene, each one carrying the thought on.
- **Clear and straightforward.** One idea per scene, 8 to 20 seconds of narration per scene, about 30 to 40 scenes.
- **Real captures wherever one is possible:** the open-source game running offline, the real tool attached to it, the
  real output of a small program written for the episode. Diagrams (cells, cards, tiles) explain; captures prove.
- **Every episode ends with** a recap scene, a practice scene (a program the viewer compiles, or a task in the practice
  game) and a "next time" scene that teases the next episode by its real title.
- The look is the kit's: pale teal paper, dark teal ink, orange accents. Do not restyle it.

## The season

| # | Folder | Title on YouTube | Site lessons it merges | Teases next as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ep01-bytes-behind-the-health-bar` | What 100 Health Really Looks Like in Memory | 1.1, 1.2 | Why the Address Changes |
| 2 | `ep02-why-the-address-changes` | Why the Health Address Changes Every Restart | 1.3, 1.4 | Read One Line of Assembly |
| 3 | `ep03-read-one-line-of-assembly` | (write it) | 1.5 reading assembly, 1.7 stack and calling conventions | Inside the Files |
| 4 | `ep04-inside-the-files` | (write it) | 1.6 hex editing files, 1.8 PE, processes and WinAPI | Your First Memory Scan |
| 5 | `ep05-your-first-memory-scan` | (write it) | 2.1 first scan, 2.2 scan types and unknown values | Finding the Pointer |
| 6 | `ep06-finding-the-pointer` | (write it) | 2.3 finding pointers, 2.4 cheat tables and hotkeys | Changing the Code |
| 7 | `ep07-changing-the-code` | (write it) | 2.5 code injection and scripts, 2.6 shared code and structures | Scripts That Survive an Update |
| 8 | `ep08-scripts-that-survive-an-update` | (write it) | 2.7 floats and multipliers, 2.8 AOB and updating scripts | (end of the Cheat Engine track: tease external trainers in general terms) |

The lesson texts are in `site/_source/01-foundations/` and `site/_source/02-cheat-engine/` (Hebrew). Use them for what to
cover and in what order; write the English narration fresh. An episode may assume everything earlier episodes taught, and
nothing else. Titles follow the pattern `"<Concrete promise or question> (Game Hacking from Scratch #N)"`.

## The one rule of the series (never break it)

Practice only on open-source games played **offline** and on programs written for the episode. Never an online game,
never other players, nothing about getting past an anti-cheat. Episode 1 says this out loud; later episodes show it by
example. If a lesson's source text goes beyond that, leave that part out.

## Steps

1. **Script and captures together.** Decide the scenes, then capture exactly what each one needs (see `lab/README.md`).
   Verify every number against the live process (`lab/peek.py`) or the program's real output before it goes on screen.
2. **Practice program** in `videos/epNN-*/lab/`: small, compiles with MSVC
   (`python -c "import subprocess;print(subprocess.run(['cmd','/c',r'D:\AI\cpp-course\probes\win\build.bat','file.cpp'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout)"`
   run in that folder), output saved next to it as `<name>.out.txt`. `.exe` files are gitignored.
3. **Scaffold:** copy `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `hyperframes.json`, `package.json`, `meta.json` from `ep02-*` and replace the
   episode name in the last two. Captures go in `assets/shots/` (PNG) and `assets/clips/` (MP4).
4. **`build.py`** with `videos/tools/kit.py`: `Scene(id, narration, body=..., js=...)`. `<<word>>` in js is the moment that word
   is spoken. `python build.py` voices it (Azure, cached) and writes the HyperFrames project and `SCRIPT.md`.
   Do not edit `kit.py` for one episode; put episode-specific helpers in its `build.py`.
5. **Check:** `npm run check` must end with `Check passed` and 0 errors. Then
   `npx --yes hyperframes@0.9.61 snapshot --at <times>` and look at a frame from **every** scene. Fix overflow, overlap
   and anything unreadable.
6. **Render:** `npm run render` (about 7 minutes). Then measure the mp4 (see "Before you call it done").
7. **`YOUTUBE.md`** like episode 1's: title, description (what the episode shows, "IN THIS EPISODE" bullets, practice
   link, tools with links, the one rule, chapters with timestamps taken from `SCRIPT.md`), tags. No `<` or `>` anywhere.
8. **`thumbnail.png`** (1920x1080): same look as `ep01-*/thumbnail.png`. Its text says the half of the idea the title
   does not say.

## Captures

- Everything is in `lab/README.md`: starting the game, Cheat Engine without elevation, the Lua command channel,
  screenshots and recordings by window, and the verified AssaultCube 1.3.0.2 offsets. Add what you verify to that file.
- The screen is shared. Take the lock before any capture session and release it after:
  `python lab/lock.py acquire screen <your-episode>` ... `python lab/lock.py release screen <your-episode>`.
  Close the game and Cheat Engine before you release it.
- Crop every capture to the tool's own window and **look at it** before use. Nothing else on the desktop may appear.
- Bots: starting a bot match from the command line has not worked reliably. If a scene needs the health to drop and you
  cannot get bots, use the ammo counter (firing) as the changing value, and say so.

## Rules learned in review (the reviewer checks these)

- **Never an empty screen under narration.** The kit moves each scene's first element to 0.3 s and its first real visual
  to 1 s, but check the render anyway.
- **Every number on screen is real and from one consistent run.** If two captures show different values (ammo 20, then
  12), the narration says why.
- **A claim about this game is captured or it is cut.** "Before the match the pointer is zero" needs a capture; otherwise
  say it as a general rule ("in many games ...").
- **An example of "this address dies" must be an address that really changed** between captured runs.
- **A bracket formula is evaluated by hand:** one read per bracket pair, against the chain drawn above it.
- **Value ranges match signedness** (a `char` is not "0 to 255" on MSVC).
- **"From the description" means the link exists.** The practice program must be pushed before the episode is queued.
- **Narration matches the picture:** if the tool updates a moment after the game, say so; do not say "at the same moment".
- **The practice task can be checked** with the program as shipped.
- **The description promises only what the video teaches.**
- A code card that shortens the real file says so.
- **An element added in a fix gets an id nothing else in the scene uses** (helpers like `chain()` already take ids such as
  `@p-c2`). The kit now stops the build on duplicate ids. After any fix, look at frames of the scene you touched.
- Hex and addresses are spelled for the voice the way episodes 1 and 2 do it ("zero zero eight nine, seven eight six C").

## Before you call it done

- `Check passed`, 0 errors.
- A frame from every scene looked at.
- No bare-background stretch of 1 s or more in the mp4, no heading-only stretch of 2 s or more.
- Mean volume around -19 dB (`ffmpeg -i x.mp4 -af volumedetect -vn -f null -`).
- `SCRIPT.md`, `YOUTUBE.md` (chapters from the final `SCRIPT.md`), `thumbnail.png`, `lab/` program and output all present.
- Game and Cheat Engine closed, screen lock released.

## Publishing (not the producer's job)

Studio project `game-hacking` (`D:\AI\studio\projects\game-hacking.json`), autopilot kind `gh` (Thursdays 16:00):
`studio.py package game-hacking <ep> --thumbnail <png>`, then `autopilot.py add game-hacking <ep> --kind gh`. The
reviewer agent gives the verdict; a remake is fixed in `build.py`, re-rendered, re-packaged and resubmitted.

```

`videos/ep01-bytes-behind-the-health-bar/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

`videos/ep01-bytes-behind-the-health-bar/SCRIPT.md`:

```md
# Narration: Game Hacking from Scratch 1: The Bytes Behind the Health Bar

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–9.6) This is AssaultCube, an open-source shooter, running offline on my own machine. Health: one hundred. Ammo: twenty.
2. (9.6–16.9) Those numbers live somewhere in the game's memory. And this is what that memory really looks like.
3. (16.9–30.7) No one hundred anywhere. Just six four, zero zero, zero zero, zero zero. By the end of this video, you will read a line like that as easily as the health bar itself.
4. (30.7–37.9) This is Game Hacking from Scratch. Episode one: the bytes behind the health bar.
5. (37.9–52.7) One rule for the whole series. We only practice on things we are allowed to touch: open-source games, offline, against bots, and programs we wrote ourselves. Never online games. Never other players.
6. (52.7–63.4) Start with the smallest piece. Memory is a very long row of boxes. Each box is one byte, and every byte has its own address.
7. (63.4–70.6) A byte is eight switches, called bits. Each bit is off or on. Zero or one.
8. (70.6–81.4) Each bit has a place value, and every place is worth double the one to its right. One, two, four, eight, all the way up to one hundred twenty-eight.
9. (81.4–95.6) To store one hundred, switch on sixty-four, thirty-two, and four. Add them up: one hundred. So in binary, our health is zero one one zero, zero one zero zero.
10. (95.6–104.4) With all eight bits on, a byte holds two hundred fifty-five. That is the largest number one byte can store.
11. (104.4–114.3) Binary is exact, but nobody wants to read eight digits for every byte. So tools use hexadecimal: base sixteen.
12. (114.3–123.6) Hex has sixteen digits. Zero to nine, then A for ten, B for eleven, up to F for fifteen.
13. (123.6–139.2) And here is the trick. One hex digit is exactly four bits. So split the byte in half. Zero one one zero is six. Zero one zero zero is four. One hundred is hex six four.
14. (139.2–157.2) You don't have to trust me. Windows Calculator has a programmer mode. Type one hundred, and it shows the same number three ways. Decimal: one hundred. Hex: six four. Binary: zero one one zero, zero one zero zero.
15. (157.2–173.2) To avoid confusion, hex numbers are written with a zero x in front. Zero x one zero is not ten. It is sixteen. And zero x F F is two hundred fifty-five: a full byte in two digits.
16. (173.2–189.4) Bigger hex numbers work the same way as decimal, only the places are powers of sixteen. Zero x one F four: one times two hundred fifty-six, plus fifteen times sixteen, plus four. Five hundred.
17. (189.4–206.6) This is why every tool in this series shows memory in hex. Two digits, one byte, and the columns line up. On the left, the address of each row. In the middle, the bytes. On the right, the same bytes shown as text.
18. (206.6–218.3) So one byte tops out at two fifty-five. But ammo, money and score get much bigger than that. A program solves it by using several bytes side by side.
19. (218.3–232.9) In C and C plus plus, the type decides how many. A char is one byte. A short is two. An int is four, good for about four billion values. A long long is eight.
20. (232.9–241.8) The game stores health as a four byte integer. That is why we saw four bytes: six four, then three zeros.
21. (241.8–251.6) But look at the order. The six four comes first, and the zeros come after. If you wrote this number on paper, it would be the other way round.
22. (251.6–268.0) This is called little endian: the smallest part of the number is stored first. Take one thousand. In hex, that is three E eight. In memory, it becomes E eight, zero three, zero zero, zero zero.
23. (268.0–286.3) Here is a tiny C plus plus program that prints the bytes of any value. Int one hundred: six four, zero zero, zero zero, zero zero. Int one thousand: E eight, zero three. Exactly as predicted.
24. (286.3–300.0) And minus one? Four bytes of F F. A signed integer uses the top half of its range for negative numbers. Read those same bytes as unsigned, and you get more than four billion.
25. (300.0–312.7) Not everything is a whole number. Positions, speeds and angles need a decimal point. For those, programs use a float: four bytes with a completely different layout.
26. (312.7–325.6) A float splits its thirty-two bits into three parts. One bit for the sign, eight for the exponent, and twenty-three for the fraction. It is scientific notation, in binary.
27. (325.6–340.9) Here is my real position in the game, in Cheat Engine. X is forty-three point zero. And its bytes: zero zero, zero zero, two C, four two. Nothing in there looks like forty-three.
28. (340.9–352.5) Now the important part. Read those same four bytes as an integer, and you get one billion, one hundred ten million. Same bytes. Different number.
29. (352.5–364.8) It works the other way too. Health is one hundred. Read its bytes as a float, and you get one point four, times ten to the minus forty-three. Practically zero.
30. (364.8–373.0) Memory does not store types. It only stores bytes. The type is a decision made by whoever is reading.
31. (373.0–386.4) Even text works this way. My player name is pixel. In memory, it is five bytes: seven zero, six nine, seven eight, six five, six C. One number per letter.
32. (386.4–401.9) Let's watch it live. On top, the game. I have already fired a few rounds, so the magazine is at twelve. Below it, Cheat Engine, an open-source memory scanner, showing the magazine's address and its raw bytes.
33. (401.9–418.4) I fire a few rounds. The counter on screen drops, and the bytes in memory drop with it. Cheat Engine re-reads the value a few times a second, so it follows a moment behind. The number on your screen is just a picture of those bytes.
34. (418.4–430.7) This is why every memory scanner asks you for a value type before it searches. Pick four bytes when the game uses a float, and you will find nothing, even though the value is right there.
35. (430.7–445.7) So here is your cheat sheet. Whole numbers like health and ammo: usually four bytes. Anything with a decimal point: float. Not sure? Try four bytes first, then float, then the rest.
36. (445.7–464.9) Let's recap. A byte is eight bits, and holds zero to two fifty-five. Hex writes one byte as two digits. Bigger numbers use more bytes, stored smallest part first. And the same bytes mean different things, depending on the type you read them as.
37. (464.9–477.1) Your practice for this episode. Compile the little program from the description, and before you run it, predict the bytes of the integer three hundred. Then check yourself.
38. (477.1–490.3) Next time: you find the health address, restart the game, and it is gone. Why the address changes, and how pointers lead you back to it. See you there.

```

# YouTube package: Game Hacking from Scratch #1

**Title:** What 100 Health Really Looks Like in Memory (Game Hacking from Scratch #1)

**Thumbnail:** `thumbnail.png`

**Description:**

Game Hacking from Scratch, Episode 1. Your health bar says 100. The game's memory says 64 00 00 00. This episode teaches you to read that line: bits, bytes, hex, data types, little endian and floats, shown on a real open-source game running offline.

📚 IN THIS EPISODE
✅ Bits, bytes and why one byte stops at 255
✅ Hexadecimal: one byte, two digits (100 = 0x64)
✅ How to read a memory viewer: address, bytes, text
✅ char, short, int, long long: the type decides the size
✅ Little endian: why 1000 is stored as E8 03 00 00
✅ Floats, and why the same bytes can be two different numbers
✅ Why every memory scanner asks you for a value type

🧪 PRACTICE
Compile bytes.cpp and predict the bytes of the integer 300 before you run it:

Everything in this series is practiced on open-source games, offline, against bots, and on programs we wrote ourselves. Never on online games, never against other players.

"""Game Hacking from Scratch, episode 1: The Bytes Behind the Health Bar (number bases + data types).

Long-form YouTube episode. Every screenshot and recording is real: AssaultCube 1.3.0.2 (open source) running offline,
Cheat Engine attached to it, Windows Calculator, and the output of lab/bytes.cpp.   Run: python build.py
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "tools"))
from kit import Scene, Shot, bar, build, card, cells, fit_clip, tag, term, tile, txt  # noqa: E402,F401

A = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "assets"
MV = (0, 128, 902, 330)            # memory viewer: the hex pane
LIST = (0, 596, 902, 334)          # Cheat Engine: the address list
ROW = {"health": 620, "health_raw": 644, "health_byte": 668, "health_float": 693, "ammo": 717, "ammo_raw": 741, "reserve": 765,
       "pos": 789, "pos_raw": 813, "pos_int": 837, "name": 861, "name_raw": 885}   # top of each row in ce_table.png


def mv(name="mv_health", y=230, crop=MV):
    return Shot("@p-mv", A / f"shots/{name}.png", 120, y, 1680, crop=crop)


def table(y=250):
    return Shot("@p-ce", A / "shots/ce_table.png", 120, y, 1680, crop=LIST)


def row_mark(s, id, row, x=672, w=160):
    return s.mark(id, x, ROW[row], w, 24, pad=6)


BITS = ["0", "1", "1", "0", "0", "1", "0", "0"]
PLACES = ["128", "64", "32", "16", "8", "4", "2", "1"]
BX, BY, BS, BG = 264, 430, 150, 28          # the bit row: x, y, size, gap


def bit_row(vals=BITS, on=(), y=BY):
    return cells("@p-b", BX, y, vals, size=BS, gap=BG, on=on)


def place_row(y=BY - 90):
    return "".join(txt(f"@p-pv{i}", BX + i * (BS + BG), y, v, "m", fs=50, w=BS, align="center") for i, v in enumerate(PLACES))


ONE = ["0", "0", "1", "0", "0", "0", "0", "0"]

OUT = ["&gt; bytes.exe",
       'int 100         <span class="hi">64 00 00 00</span>',
       'int 1000        <span class="hi">E8 03 00 00</span>',
       'int -1          <span class="hi">FF FF FF FF</span>',
       'float 43.0      <span class="hi">00 00 2C 42</span>']

GAME = (1582, 890)
CEV = (898, 350)


def live_game(still=False):
    s = Shot("@p-g", A / ("shots/live_game.png" if still else "clips/shoot_game.mp4"), 410, 50, 1100, size=GAME)
    return s


def live_ce(still=False):
    return Shot("@p-c", A / ("shots/live_ce.png" if still else "clips/shoot_ce.mp4"), 110, 760, 1700, crop=(0, 124, 898, 50), size=CEV)


def live_media(dur):
    g, c = live_game(), live_ce()
    g.path = fit_clip(A / "clips/shoot_game.mp4", dur, 2.6)
    c.path = fit_clip(A / "clips/shoot_ce.mp4", dur, 2.6)
    g.src, c.src = f"assets/clips/{g.path.name}", f"assets/clips/{c.path.name}"
    return g.video(0, dur) + c.video(0, dur)

`videos/ep01-bytes-behind-the-health-bar/lab/bytes.cpp`:

```cpp
// Episode 1 practice program: print the bytes a value really occupies in memory.
#include <cstdio>
#include <cstring>

template <class T>
void dump(const char* label, T value) {
    unsigned char bytes[sizeof(T)];
    std::memcpy(bytes, &value, sizeof(T));
    std::printf("%-16s", label);
    for (unsigned char b : bytes) std::printf("%02X ", b);
    std::printf("\n");
}

int main() {
    dump("char 100", (char)100);
    dump("short 100", (short)100);
    dump("int 100", 100);
    dump("int 1000", 1000);
    dump("int 300", 300);        // the practice question: predict this line first
    dump("int -1", -1);
    dump("float 100.0", 100.0f);
    dump("float 43.0", 43.0f);
    dump("double 43.0", 43.0);

    int health = 100;
    float as_float;
    std::memcpy(&as_float, &health, 4);          // same four bytes, read as a float
    std::printf("int 100 read as a float: %g\n", as_float);

    float x = 43.0f;
    int as_int;
    std::memcpy(&as_int, &x, 4);                 // same four bytes, read as an integer
    std::printf("float 43.0 read as an int: %d\n", as_int);
}

`videos/ep02-why-the-address-changes/AGENTS.md`:

```md
# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

## Documentation

**For quick reference**, use the local CLI docs command (no network required):

```bash
npx hyperframes docs <topic>
```

Topics: `data-attributes`, `gsap`, `compositions`, `rendering`, `examples`, `troubleshooting`

**For full documentation**, discover pages via the machine-readable index — do NOT guess URLs:

```
https://hyperframes.heygen.com/llms.txt
```

## Project Structure

- `index.html` — main composition (root timeline)
- `compositions/` — sub-compositions referenced via `data-composition-src`
- `meta.json` — project metadata (id, name)
- `transcript.json` — whisper word-level transcript (if generated)

## Linting — ALWAYS RUN AFTER CHANGES

After creating or editing any `.html` composition, **always** run the full check before considering the task complete:

```bash
npm run check
```

Fix all errors before presenting the result. Warnings should be reviewed before rendering.

Then look at what you changed: `npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>` (or `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`) at the moments you edited, and read the frames before you reply. A passing check does not show how it looks.

## Key Rules

1. Every timed element needs `data-start` and a duration. `data-start` is what marks it as timed; `data-track-index` is an optional Studio display lane the render never reads
2. Give timed visual elements `class="clip"`. The framework keys visibility off `data-start`, not the class, but the shared `.clip` CSS is what gives a scene its full-frame box, and `lint` warns without it
3. Register one paused root timeline per composition on `window.__timelines`:
   ```js
   window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {};
   window.__timelines["composition-id"] = gsap.timeline({ paused: true });
   ```
   Scene timelines manually added to this root must not be paused. A paused
   child does not advance when the root is seeked. The runtime activates
   registered composition siblings, not arbitrary nested scene timelines.
4. A video with sound keeps it on the `<video>` (`data-has-audio="true"`, no `muted`). Use a separate `<audio>` for music, voiceover, replacement audio, J/L cuts, or audio detached in Studio. Silent footage and b-roll: `muted`.
5. Sub-compositions use `data-composition-src="compositions/file.html"` to reference other HTML files
6. Only deterministic logic — no `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()`, no network fetches

```

# HyperFrames Composition Project

This folder is a [HyperFrames](https://hyperframes.heygen.com) video: HTML, CSS and seekable
animations (GSAP by default) that the `hyperframes` CLI previews in the browser and renders to
MP4.

## Skills — read these first

**Invoke the relevant skill before writing or modifying compositions.** Skills encode framework-specific patterns (e.g., `window.__timelines` registration, `data-*` attribute semantics, shader-compatible CSS rules) that generic web docs don't cover, so compositions written without them break.

**Doing anything with HyperFrames?** Start at `/hyperframes`. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (each kind of film, story, motion, look, sound, review, captions, overlays). Read it first, especially when there's no project context to orient you.

- `/hyperframes` — read first for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays. Holds the render contract and the work loop.
- `/hyperframes-cli` — the CLI by job: scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render, publish, project history.
- `/hyperframes-registry` — ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source. Search it before hand-building any named visual.
- `/media-use` — get or make any media (music, sound effects, images, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades) and mix placed audio.
- `/reverse-any-video` — rebuild any video file as an editable HyperFrames project and check it against the original frame by frame (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/style-sampling` — make a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles (HyperFrames Pro).
- `/figma` — bring a Figma design, frame, logo or brand into a video.
- `/slideshow` — a presentation or pitch deck. Output is a navigable deck, not a rendered MP4.
- `/remotion-to-hyperframes` — bring existing video code or footage into HyperFrames (Remotion first; also Motion Canvas, Lottie, Three.js, canvas, or renders from other tools) and verify it frame by frame against the original.

**Changing how real footage or images look or reveal?** Load `/media-use` and read its `references/media-treatments.md` before editing, even when the request only says dark, flat, boring, retro, private, or “make the reveal cooler.” It governs how footage is treated, never whether media may be used. Use canonical media treatments and seek-safe motion; do not improvise equivalent CSS/SVG filters or overlays.

> **Tailwind v4 projects** (`hyperframes init --tailwind`): see `hyperframes-cli/references/init-and-scaffold.md` (Tailwind).

> **Using a HyperFrames plugin?** Load skills from that installed bundle and follow
> its `hyperframes/references/plugin-installation.md` execution rules. The person updates
> the plugin through its plugin manager; the standalone commands below do not apply.
>
> **Standalone skill missing or stale?** Installing and updating skills is the person's step:
> tell them which skill is missing or stale, and do not run the install yourself. For the user:
> `npx hyperframes skills update <name>` installs/refreshes that skill, and bare
> `npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes the core set plus everything already installed —
> neither pulls the full set. Newly installed skills load in a new agent session.

## Commands

```bash
npm run dev          # human-operated foreground preview (blocks until stopped)
npx hyperframes preview --background  # agent-safe persistent Studio preview
npx hyperframes preview --status      # verify the persistent preview is listening
npx hyperframes preview --stop        # stop it when review is finished
npm run check        # lint + runtime + layout + motion + contrast (one command)
npx hyperframes snapshot --at 1,3,5  # PNG frames at those seconds, to look at before rendering
npm run render       # render to MP4
npm run publish      # publish and get a shareable link
npx hyperframes lint --verbose  # include info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json     # machine-readable output for CI
npx hyperframes docs <topic> # reference docs in terminal
```

> **Agents must use `npx hyperframes preview --background` for Studio handoff.** Do not rely
> on a shell/tool `run_in_background` wrapper around `npm run dev`: that foreground process
> remains owned by the invoking session and can disappear while the browser stays open,
> leaving refreshes at `ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`. Verify with `preview --status`. The desktop
> app can't edit the project while this preview runs, so `npx hyperframes open` stops it first.
> If you hand the project to the app another way, run `preview --stop` before you do. Otherwise keep it
> alive through review, and stop it explicitly with `preview --stop` afterward.

> **Back from the desktop app.** Once this project was opened in the HyperFrames desktop app, run `npx hyperframes catch-up` before your next change here: it lists what the person asked Framey in the app and which files changed since.

> **Pinned CLI version.** These scripts pin an exact `hyperframes@X.Y.Z` so this project re-renders identically over time. Weeks later that pin lags fixes shipped since. To move up: `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project . --check` (shows the delta), then `npx hyperframes@latest upgrade --project .` to rewrite the pins. Always unpinned — the pinned script re-runs the old version against itself.

```md
# Narration: Game Hacking from Scratch 2: Why the Address Changes

Voiced with Azure Speech (en-US-AvaMultilingualNeural, rate -4%). Generated by build.py.

1. (0.0–10.4) Last episode, we found our player's health at this address. Zero zero eight nine, seven eight six C. One hundred, right there.
2. (10.4–22.1) So I close the game, start it again, and look at the same address. Eight thousand, two hundred ninety-two. That is not my health. That is garbage.
3. (22.1–37.3) Nothing broke. My player simply moved. And yet the game itself never loses it. By the end of this episode, you will know how the game finds its player, and how to find it the same way, on every single run.
4. (37.3–44.2) This is Game Hacking from Scratch. Episode two: why the address changes.
5. (44.2–54.5) First, the evidence. I started the game three times, and wrote down where the health was. Three runs. Three different addresses.
6. (54.5–71.0) To see why, we need the map. Every process gets its own address space. For a thirty-two bit game like this one, that is four gigabytes of addresses, from zero, all the way up to F F F F, F F F F.
7. (71.0–81.2) And it is private. The same address in two programs is two completely different places. That is why it is called virtual memory.
8. (81.2–93.2) This is the real map of our game, in Cheat Engine's memory regions view. Every row is one region: where it starts, what you are allowed to do there, and how big it is.
9. (93.2–111.3) Find address four hundred thousand, in hex. This is the game's own file, loaded into memory: its module. First the code: execute and read. Then constants: read only. Then global variables: read and write.
10. (111.3–122.9) Those permissions are enforced by the processor. Write to a read only page, or try to run data as code, and the program crashes with an access violation.
11. (122.9–134.2) Further down is the heap: private, read and write. This is where a program creates things while it runs. Bullets, enemies, and your player.
12. (134.2–147.2) And that is the answer. The player object is created on the heap while the game runs. Wherever there is free space at that moment, that is where it goes. Different run, different spot.
13. (147.2–167.6) You can watch this with a few lines of C plus plus. This program creates a player on the heap, and prints where things live. I ran it three times. The heap address is different every time. But look at the global variable: base plus two two B seven zero, on every run.
14. (167.6–188.1) A module has a base address, and everything inside it sits at a fixed offset from that base. Windows is free to move the base, usually when the machine restarts. That is A S L R: address space layout randomization. But base plus offset always lands on the same variable.
15. (188.1–197.2) So here is the first rule of this series. Never save a raw address. Save the module name, and the offset.
16. (197.2–211.6) Now, how does the game find a player that keeps moving? It keeps a note. Somewhere in its global data, at a fixed offset, it stores the player's current address. That note is called a pointer.
17. (211.6–223.8) A pointer is not magic. It is just a number. Four bytes in a thirty-two bit game, eight in a sixty-four bit one. And that number happens to be an address.
18. (223.8–245.9) Here it is, for real. At the game's base plus one seven E zero A eight, there are four bytes. F zero, six zero, nine seven, zero zero. Little endian, remember? Flip them: zero zero nine seven, six zero F zero. That is where my player is, right now.
19. (245.9–262.9) The player is a structure: a block of fields in a fixed order. Health is always the same distance from the start: E C. Ammo: one four zero. Those offsets were decided when the game was compiled. They never change between runs.
20. (262.9–281.1) So the recipe has two steps. Read the pointer. Then add the offset. Zero zero nine seven, six zero F zero, plus E C, is zero zero nine seven, six one D C. And at that address: one hundred.
21. (281.1–297.4) Cheat Engine can do that for us. This row uses the pointer instead of a raw address, and it shows one hundred. The top two rows are the addresses from the earlier runs. Wrong values. The pointer row survives every restart.
22. (297.4–309.9) One warning. Order matters. Read first, then add. If you add the offset to the pointer's own address and then read, you land somewhere else in the module, and get nonsense.
23. (309.9–323.6) Real games chain several of these. In AssaultCube, the player holds a pointer to its current weapon. The weapon holds a pointer to its ammo. Read, add, read, add.
24. (323.6–341.0) With real numbers from this run. Base plus one seven E zero A eight gives the player. Player plus three six four gives the weapon. Weapon plus one four gives the address of the ammo. One last read, at that address: twenty.
25. (341.0–351.6) You will see this written with square brackets. A pair of brackets means: read what is stored at this address. So the whole chain fits on one line.
26. (351.6–372.5) One more thing. A pointer can also hold zero. In many games, before a match starts, there is no player yet. Follow a zero pointer and you read address zero, which is never mapped. So every tool, and every program you write, should check for zero, and stop.
27. (372.5–385.1) How do you discover a pointer like this, in a game you have never seen? That is a skill of its own, and we will get there in the Cheat Engine episodes. Today was about knowing what you are looking for.
28. (385.1–405.1) Let's recap. Every process has its own virtual address space, split into regions with permissions. The module sits at a base. The heap moves on every run. A pointer is a number that holds an address. And a pointer chain is the path the game itself walks to its own data.
29. (405.1–418.5) Your practice. Compile where dot C P P from the description, run it three times, and write down what moves and what stays. Then restart your computer, and run it once more.
30. (418.5–430.0) Next time, we open the code itself: what one line of assembly says, and where a function keeps its arguments. See you there.

```

# YouTube package: Game Hacking from Scratch #2

**Title:** Why the Health Address Changes Every Restart (Game Hacking from Scratch #2)

**Thumbnail:** `thumbnail.png`

**Description:**

Game Hacking from Scratch, Episode 2. You find the health address, restart the game, and it holds garbage. Nothing broke: the player moved. This episode shows the real memory map of a running game, why the heap moves on every run, and how a pointer chain leads you back to the same value every time.

📚 IN THIS EPISODE
✅ Virtual memory: every process gets its own address space
✅ Reading a real memory map: regions, permissions, sizes
✅ The module and the heap, and which of them moves
✅ Base + offset, and what ASLR changes
✅ A pointer is just a number that holds an address
✅ Pointer chains with real numbers: player, weapon, ammo
✅ The bracket notation, and why a zero pointer means stop

🧪 PRACTICE
Compile where.cpp, run it three times and write down what moves and what stays:

⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Everything in this series is practiced on open-source games, offline, against bots, and on programs we wrote ourselves. Never on online games, never against other players.

`videos/ep02-why-the-address-changes/build.py`:

```py
"""Game Hacking from Scratch, episode 2: Why the Address Changes (virtual memory + pointers and pointer chains).

Long-form YouTube episode. Every screenshot and number is real: AssaultCube 1.3.0.2 (open source) started three times on this
machine, Cheat Engine's memory regions and memory viewer, and three runs of lab/where.cpp.   Run: python build.py
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "tools"))
from kit import Scene, Shot, bar, build, card, cells, tag, term, tile, txt  # noqa: E402,F401

A = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "assets"
LIST = (0, 596, 902, 150)              # Cheat Engine address list: header + five rows
ROWS = [620, 644, 668, 693, 717]       # top of each row in table_run1.png
LIST3 = (0, 624, 902, 150)             # the run-3 screenshot: its list sits 28 px lower
ROWS3 = [r + 28 for r in ROWS]
MV = (0, 128, 902, 200)


def table(name, y=250, crop=None):
    crop = crop or (LIST3 if name.startswith("ep02") else LIST)
    return Shot("@p-ce", A / f"shots/{name}.png", 120, y, 1680, crop=crop)


def regions(name, crop, y=230):
    return Shot("@p-rg", A / f"shots/{name}.png", 120, y, 1680, crop=crop)


REG_MOD = (0, 40, 1284, 390)
REG_HEAP = (0, 330, 1284, 240)

RUNS = ["0089786C", "00965E7C", "009761DC"]

WHERE = ['<span class="dimc">--- run 1</span>',
         'module base     7FF7D6F10000',
         '&amp;g_player       7FF7D6F32B70  <span class="hi">= base + 22B70</span>',
         'player (heap)   <span class="hi">01C5484C7E40</span>',
         '<span class="dimc">--- run 2</span>',
         'module base     7FF7D6F10000',
         '&amp;g_player       7FF7D6F32B70  <span class="hi">= base + 22B70</span>',
         'player (heap)   <span class="hi">01FE8CB00680</span>',
         '<span class="dimc">--- run 3</span>',

`videos/ep02-why-the-address-changes/lab/where.cpp`:

```cpp
// Episode 2 practice program: where do things live, and does it change between runs?
#include <cstdio>
#include <windows.h>

struct Player {
    int health = 100;
    int ammo = 20;
};

Player* g_player = nullptr;   // a global pointer: it lives inside the module

int main() {
    g_player = new Player;    // the player itself lives on the heap
    int local = 7;            // a local variable lives on the stack

    auto base = (unsigned long long)GetModuleHandle(nullptr);
    auto global = (unsigned long long)&g_player;

    std::printf("module base       %012llX\n", base);
    std::printf("&g_player         %012llX   = base + %llX\n", global, global - base);
    std::printf("player (heap)     %012llX\n", (unsigned long long)g_player);
    std::printf("local (stack)     %012llX\n", (unsigned long long)&local);
    std::printf("health through the pointer: %d\n", g_player->health);
}
